transcript.speaker: Lucy Milligan
transcript.text: Welcome back to World Stories. I'm Lucy Milligan, and today we talk about the terrible floods in Nepal. My guest is Emma McKinley, a British aid worker who's been helping there since the first day. Emma, thank you for coming. Can you tell us what happened on 26 August?

transcript.speaker: Emma McKinley
transcript.text: Thank you, Lucy. It was a morning that nobody here will forget. I was working in a district called Nuwakot — that's N-U-W-A-K-O-T. At first everything was quiet and normal. People were eating breakfast, and children were getting ready for school. The sky was clear and blue, and the river was calm. Then, just before ten thirty, we heard this very loud, deep noise. It sounded like thunder, but there wasn't a cloud in the sky. We all stopped and looked at each other, and nobody knew what it was.

transcript.speaker: Lucy Milligan
transcript.text: And then what happened?

transcript.speaker: Emma McKinley
transcript.text: Then the water came. But it was not a normal flood. A normal flood rises slowly, so you have time to move to higher ground. This was different. It was like a wall — a wall of water, mud, rocks and broken ice that moved very fast down the valley. It swept everything out of its path in seconds. There was no time to run, and no time to warn anyone. One minute there was a village, and the next there was just mud and water.

transcript.speaker: Lucy Milligan
transcript.text: You mentioned broken ice. Where did that come from?

transcript.speaker: Emma McKinley
transcript.text: Later, we learned that part of a glacier had broken. A glacier is a huge, slow river of ice that forms high up on the mountains. This one was on a peak called Langtang Lirung — that's L-A-N-G-T-A-N-G for Langtang and L-I-R-U-N-G for Lirung. It sits right on the border with China. When the ice broke away, it rushed down the slopes, picked up rocks and mud, and poured into the Trishuli river — T-R-I-S-H-U-L-I. The water kept moving for about a hundred kilometres before it slowed down.

transcript.speaker: Lucy Milligan
transcript.text: So one moment everything was calm, and the next there was a wall of water.

transcript.speaker: Emma McKinley
transcript.text: Exactly. And it moved very fast. For the first twenty-two kilometres, it travelled at about one hundred and ninety kilometres an hour — that's faster than a car on a motorway. And that is why there was nothing anyone could do. The whole thing, from the mountains to the villages, happened in a few minutes.

transcript.speaker: Lucy Milligan
transcript.text: So what actually caused the glacier to break? At first, many people said it was an earthquake, didn't they?

transcript.speaker: Emma McKinley
transcript.text: Yes, they did, and it's easy to see why. When the glacier collapsed, the US Geological Survey recorded it as a small tremor — about four point four on the Richter scale. So for a day or two, many people believed there had been an earthquake, and that the earthquake had caused a landslide. It was easy to think that, because a big movement makes vibrations, and the instruments pick them up.

transcript.speaker: Lucy Milligan
transcript.text: But the truth was different, wasn't it?

transcript.speaker: Emma McKinley
transcript.text: Yes, it was. After scientists studied the satellite images and went to look at the area, they realised the real cause. It was a glacial collapse. A very large piece of ice and rock on top of the mountain broke off and fell. It wasn't an earthquake at all — the earthquake reading was the result of the collapse, not the cause.

transcript.speaker: Lucy Milligan
transcript.text: And why does this happen? Why now, this year?

transcript.speaker: Emma McKinley
transcript.text: The main reason is climate change. Our planet is getting warmer, so the glaciers in the Himalayas are melting. As they melt, they get weaker and thinner. Sometimes a big piece breaks away all at once, without any warning. That is exactly what happened here. It isn't one sudden event — it's the result of years of slow, steady warming.

transcript.speaker: Lucy Milligan
transcript.text: But surely scientists could see this coming and warn people in advance?

transcript.speaker: Emma McKinley
transcript.text: Not really, and that's the terrible problem. The Himalayas are enormous, and many of these glaciers are in very remote places. The weather that day was calm and clear. Scientists know that thousands of glaciers are melting, but they cannot say which one will be the next to break, or exactly when. There are too many mountains, and they change very slowly until, suddenly, they change all at once.

transcript.speaker: Lucy Milligan
transcript.text: And the effects were terrible, weren't they?

transcript.speaker: Emma McKinley
transcript.text: Yes, they were. In the first week, more than a thousand people had lost their lives, and thousands more were still missing. Many of those who died were women and children. In total, about sixty-five thousand people were affected by the flood and the mud. That's roughly the same as a small city, suddenly left with nothing.

transcript.speaker: Lucy Milligan
transcript.text: That's hard to imagine. And what about the buildings and the roads?

transcript.speaker: Emma McKinley
transcript.text: The flood swept away almost everything in its path. Hundreds of homes were destroyed, along with roads and bridges, so many villages became cut off from the rest of the country. Nineteen schools were destroyed, which means around ten thousand children lost their classrooms overnight. It also blocked the tunnels of hydroelectric power stations — big plants that use the rivers to make electricity — so large parts of the country had no power.

transcript.speaker: Lucy Milligan
transcript.text: And it wasn't only the villages, was it?

transcript.speaker: Emma McKinley
transcript.text: No. In fact, it destroyed the town of Gyirong — G-Y-I-R-O-N-G — which is a major port and a very important trade crossing on the border with China. So a key route between the two countries was wiped out. The total cost of the damage is now over two hundred billion rupees, which is more than a billion US dollars. And sadly, I expect that figure will rise as the rescue continues.

transcript.speaker: Lucy Milligan
transcript.text: So what is happening now? And is the danger over?

transcript.speaker: Emma McKinley
transcript.text: I'm afraid the answer is no. Right now, rescue teams are still working to reach people, and there is still a very serious risk. In one place, two hundred and seventy-nine workers were trapped inside the tunnels of a hydropower plant, and rescuers brought them out one by one. But the biggest worry is a new lake that has formed.

transcript.speaker: Lucy Milligan
transcript.text: A new lake? That sounds strange. Where did that come from?

transcript.speaker: Emma McKinley
transcript.text: When the glacier collapsed, it left huge amounts of rock, ice and debris that blocked the river upstream. That material has created what we call a barrier lake — really, a natural dam across the river. The lake is still growing, and water is building up behind it day by day. If that dam of rock and ice breaks, it would send another wall of water down the valley, and it would hit many of the same villages again. So the danger is definitely not over.

transcript.speaker: Lucy Milligan
transcript.text: That's frightening. And this risk isn't only in Nepal, is it? Many places in Asia face the same danger.

transcript.speaker: Emma McKinley
transcript.text: That's exactly right. Nepal is not alone. As the planet gets warmer, the risk of heavy rain and terrible flooding is growing across Asia. One country facing a very serious danger is Thailand. Thailand is one of the most flood-affected countries in the world — a huge part of Bangkok, the capital, sits on low, flat land that is not far above the sea. So when the water comes, there is very little space for it to go.

transcript.speaker: Lucy Milligan
transcript.text: And has Thailand already had bad floods?

transcript.speaker: Emma McKinley
transcript.text: Yes, sadly. In 2011, Thailand had a terrible flood. More than eight hundred people died, and over thirteen million people were affected. Large parts of the country were under water for weeks. And scientists warn that, as the climate changes, these floods will get worse — there will be more, and they will be stronger. Some experts believe the number of people affected in Thailand could double by 2030. So this is not just one sad event in Nepal — it is a problem that will affect millions of lives across Asia.

transcript.speaker: Lucy Milligan
transcript.text: So this is really a climate story, not only a Nepal story.

transcript.speaker: Emma McKinley
transcript.text: Exactly. And here is the sad truth. Countries like Nepal and Thailand have caused very little of this problem, yet they are among the first to feel it. They don't have the money, or the strong buildings, to protect themselves. That is why we all need to act — not only to help them recover, but to stop the planet getting any warmer. If we don't, events like this will happen again and again.
